In a mining boarding house out west, Emmett Rusk's mother signed her son over to the banker Barrow after a defaulted lodger's mine deed made the family rich. The boy drove his sled into Barrow's stomach and was taken east away from his parents anyway.

On his twenty-fifth birthday Emmett took control of the fortune and told Barrow that of all his holdings he wanted to run a failing city newspaper, the Clarion. He moved into the Clarion, installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. Emmett hired away the entire staff of the rival paper and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line.

He returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. A run of breakfast-table scenes charted the marriage cooling into silence behind separate newspapers. Emmett met the shopgirl Nora Kell on the street with mud on his coat and started visiting her rooms in secret. Mid-campaign for governor, the party boss Halloran brought Adele to Nora's rooms and threatened exposure, and Emmett refused to withdraw. He lost the election, Devlin asked to be transferred to another city, and the marriage collapsed.

Emmett married Nora and forced her into an opera career for which she had no voice. Nora's debut was a humiliation, and a drunk Devlin began the savage review that Emmett finished, printed, and fired him for. Nora swallowed poison rather than sing again, and Emmett finally let her stop. He shut Nora away in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where she worked jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall. After a joyless beach picnic and a quarrel, Nora packed and left him.

Emmett wrecked Nora's bedroom, found a glass snow globe, murmured "Bluebell", and carried it past the endless mirrors. Alone at Silvermount, Emmett died with the word "Bluebell" on his lips and dropped the snow globe on the floor. A newsreel obituary recapped Emmett's public life and closed without explaining his last word.

The reporter Nash was sent to find out what "Bluebell" means and was turned away by a drunk Nora in a seaside nightclub. Nash read Barrow's memoir and interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora and the butler Colm before concluding that no single word explains a life, as workmen shoveled a sled marked Bluebell into the furnace.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war pressed a gold watch into the palm of a young boy, explaining that the boy's father had kept it hidden through the long years of captivity. The boy, Denny, never forgot the weight of it.

Hitmen Rollo and Marcus drove across the city, arguing about foreign drug laws and what people called fast food abroad. Outside their target's flat they waited in the corridor, still bickering over whether a foot massage was worth killing a man for. Inside, Marcus recited a short passage of scripture before they shot young Tobin for double-crossing their employer Otis and recovered the briefcase. A fourth man hidden in the bathroom emptied a revolver at them without hitting either; Marcus called it divine intervention. Back in the car Rollo's gun went off and blew the head clean off their passenger Del. Marcus parked the bloodied car at his friend Warren's house, where a fixer directed the cleanup and handed them fresh clothes.

Over breakfast in a coffee shop two small-time robbers decided on the spot to hold up the diner they were sitting in. Marcus talked the robber down mid-holdup, handed over his own wallet, kept the briefcase, and let the couple walk out. The two hitmen delivered the case to Otis at his bar, where Otis was paying the ageing boxer Denny to take a dive in the fifth.

Rollo bought heroin from his dealer Kip and shot up before his night out. He took Otis's wife Nadia to a themed diner where they won the dance contest. Later Nadia snorted Rollo's heroin, overdosed, and was revived by an adrenaline shot to the heart on the dealer's living-room floor.

Denny double-crossed Otis, won the fight and killed his opponent in the ring, then escaped in a taxi. Hiding in a motel with his girlfriend Marielle, he discovered she had left his father's watch behind in his flat. He returned for it and shot Rollo dead with a submachine gun left on the kitchen counter.

Denny and Otis collided in the street, crashed, and were taken prisoner in the basement of a pawnshop. Denny broke free, came back with a sword from the shop wall while one of their captors was raping Otis, and Otis declared them square on condition Denny leave town. Denny collected Marielle and rode out of the city on a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop.

They met at a beach party in the seaside town at the end of the rail line, two strangers drawn to the same empty house on the shore. Tobias forced the lock; Ivy laughed as they stepped inside the damp rooms that smelled of salt and abandonment. Over the next two years they fell in love in ordinary places: skating the ice on the frozen river until their ankles burned, sharing bowls at the noodle house where the steam fogged the windows, kissing in the back row of the drive-in while the soundtrack washed over them.  

Then the relationship curdled. Her drinking became the subject of every argument; his silence and withholding became hers. One night she came home drunk and admitted she had dented his car. The fight that followed was the last. She walked out for good, slamming the door on everything they had built.  

Ivy hired a memory-erasure clinic and paid to have every trace of Tobias removed from her mind. Weeks later Tobias wandered into the bookshop where she worked and found her treating him as a stranger, leaning across the counter to flirt with a young man named Peck. Nina and Grady showed him the form letter from the clinic. He went straight to its director, Dr. Hallam, and demanded the same procedure.  

Tobias boxed every object that still carried her—ticket stubs, a scarf, the cracked mug from the noodle house—so the technicians could map the memories attached to them. That night Dell and Peck ran the overnight erasure in his flat. While the machines hummed, Peck quietly pocketed the mementos, planning to use them on Ivy later.  

Inside his own head Tobias watched the most recent and ugliest memories dissolve first: the dented fender, the slammed door, the recriminations. When the process reached the memories he still loved, he changed his mind. He tried to smuggle Ivy into scenes she had never been part of, grafting her face onto childhood summers and solitary walks. The map went off the rails. Dell and the receptionist Rosa got high on Tobias’s bed and lost track of the procedure entirely.  

Dr. Hallam arrived to re-map the erasure. Rosa kissed him in the hallway; a moment later his wife appeared and revealed that Rosa’s own affair with him had already been erased, leaving her with nothing but residual longing. In the last surviving memory—the empty house on the shore—Tobias and Ivy stood once more among the salt-stained walls. They said goodbye. She told him to meet her at the beach.  

The erasure completed. Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy had ever existed. On an impulse he could not account for he skipped work, took the train to the coast, and found her standing alone on the frozen sand. They drove back to the city together. At her building she invited him up to her flat.  

That same day Rosa quit the clinic and mailed the files and session tapes back to every patient on the books. Tobias and Ivy sat on her floor and listened to their own recorded voices tearing each other apart. She ran from the room, then came back, eyes red. They looked at each other for a long time and agreed to try anyway.

Nadir stood in the gun shop with his daughter Sahar while the dealer mocked his accent and sold him the handgun anyway. That same night Trey and Kwame forced prosecutor Halstead out of his car outside a restaurant and drove off laughing. Across town Officer Boyle pulled over the Hobarts, groped Renee in front of her husband Clay, then waved them on with a warning. Boyle’s partner Voss went straight to their commander and asked for a new patrol car rather than keep riding with a racist.

Locksmith Mateo changed the Halsteads’ locks while Paula loudly assumed he was a gang member about to sell her keys. Later he replaced the lock on Nadir’s shop and warned that the door itself was broken; Nadir accused him of running a con. Boyle pleaded with health-insurance clerk Delia Frank for treatment for his father and was refused. Overnight Nadir’s shop was smashed and looted; the insurer denied the claim because he had ignored the warning about the door.

Renee ended up trapped upside down in a burning wreck. Boyle, the same officer who had assaulted her, crawled in through the flames and dragged her free. Elsewhere Trey and Kwame ran down a shopkeeper named Pham and dumped him outside a hospital. Clay was stopped mid-carjacking of his own car; Voss talked the other officers out of shooting him. Clay then drove Trey away from the police at speed and threw him out onto the pavement.

Nadir waited outside Mateo’s house with the gun. He fired just as Mateo’s small daughter Rosie ran into her father’s arms. The child was untouched—Sahar had bought blanks—and Nadir decided she was his angel. Voss picked up Kwame hitchhiking, misread him reaching into his pocket, shot him dead, and burned the car. Detective Isaiah Reece was called to a body dumped by the roadside and found that it was his brother Kwame. Their mother blamed Reece for never once going to look for him.

Paula fell down her stairs and told her housekeeper Alba that she was the only friend she had. Trey found Pham’s van packed with trafficked migrants and turned them loose at the docks instead of selling them. In the first snow of the year another collision started another argument in the street.

Martin Kray sat across from the claimant Elias Prine and listened to the careful gaps in his story. As an insurance investigator he had heard every variation of convenient forgetting. He ruled the memory loss psychosomatic, signed the denial, and closed the file.

Elias’s diabetic wife began testing him that same week. She asked for injection after injection, watching his face for any flicker of recognition. He gave them without remembering the last, and she died of the overdose he could not recall administering.

Months later intruders forced their way into Martin’s bathroom while he and his wife were preparing for bed. Martin killed one with a shard of mirror glass. The second struck him hard across the skull. When he woke the world refused to stay. He could form no new memories.

He built a system to survive the blankness: instant photographs annotated in black marker, notes taped to walls, facts tattooed across his body. The second attacker existed only as the initials R.M. Everything pointed toward finding him.

About a year before the stretch of days that would feel like the present, a plainclothes officer named Roy helped Martin track the real attacker to a warehouse. Martin fired the shot that ended it. Within minutes the killing itself had vanished from his mind, leaving only the tattoos and the photographs as proof that something had happened.

In a motel room he had no memory of checking into, Martin held a phone to his ear and narrated the old Prine case to an anonymous caller. He burned his wife’s hairbrush and her books in an empty field afterward, trying to force grief into a mind that could not keep it.

The caller fed him a name and a location: the drug dealer Gil Marsh. Martin found him in a derelict basement, beat him until the man could barely stand, then strangled him and photographed the body. As he died Gil whispered “Elias.” Martin could not explain the word. He changed into the dead man’s suit, took the keys to the sports car, and drove away.

Roy arrived while the Polaroids were still developing. He told Martin that Gil had been innocent, that Martin had already avenged his wife a year earlier, and that Martin himself was the man in the Prine story—the investigator who had become the claimant. Martin stared at him, then burned the photographs of Gil. On Roy’s own picture he wrote “he is lying to you” and copied down the licence plate as his next target.

He drove straight to a tattoo parlour and had the plate inked on his thigh as the sixth fact.

At her bar, Gil’s girlfriend Corinne recognised the dead man’s clothes and the car outside. She served Martin a beer the staff had spat in. Later, at her house, she hid every pen so he could leave no notes. She goaded him until he hit her, then returned bruised and named a man called Vance as the one responsible, sending Martin after him.

Martin ambushed Vance in a motel bathroom, beat him bloody, and drove him out of town at gunpoint. Corinne ran the licence plate through a friend at the vehicle registry and handed Martin the printout naming Roy Mercer.

Martin lured Roy to the same derelict building, shot him once in the head, and photographed the corpse before the blood had finished spreading.

Undercover officer Danny Roarke sat across from his handler Pruitt in the cramped safe house, repeating the fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet until the details sat in his mouth like true memory. He polished the timing, the smell of piss and bleach, the way the dealer’s knife had flashed under the stall door, until Pruitt finally nodded and sent him out.

That night Danny performed it for the boss Bram, his son Cal, and the quiet man called Mr. Ash. He let the story roll out easy, eyes half-lidded, voice low. Bram watched him the whole time, then clapped once and said he was in. From then on Danny answered to Mr. Elm.

Ren Vasco walked out of prison two days later and reported straight to Bram and Cal. They owed him for the years he had kept his mouth shut, and the debt hung in the air like cigarette smoke while they shook hands.

Over breakfast the crew argued about what a pop song on the café radio was really about and whether the waitress who kept their cups full deserved a tip. Mr. Ash said the song was about getting away clean. Cal said it was about getting caught. Nobody tipped.

Bram handed out the tree aliases. Elm, Ash, Birch, Cedar. Mr. Birch objected at once to being Mr. Birch, said it sounded soft, but Bram told him to shut it and take the name.

The robbery collapsed inside a minute. Alarms, sirens, boots on wet pavement. Mr. Ash shot his way clear of the police from the getaway car with Mr. Elm jammed in beside him, the diamonds rattling in a canvas bag on the floor.

Fleeing on foot after the car died, Mr. Elm hijacked a civilian vehicle at a red light. The terrified driver shot him in the stomach through the open window. Elm shot the man dead, dragged himself into the seat, and somehow kept the car moving until Ash caught up and took the wheel.

Ash drove the screaming Elm to the warehouse rendezvous, cradled him against the seat, and swore he was not going to die. Blood soaked through Elm’s shirt and onto Ash’s hands.

Mr. Birch arrived next, arguing that the job had been a setup with an informer inside it. While the others watched Elm bleed, Birch slipped outside and hid the diamonds under a loose paving stone behind the loading dock.

Mr. Cedar strolled in late and popped the boot of his car. Inside lay a kidnapped patrolman named Doyle, bound and gagged, eyes wide above the tape. Cedar dumped him on the concrete floor.

Left alone with the bound officer, Mr. Cedar turned up a radio oldie, danced a slow circle around Doyle, then cut off his ear with a folding knife and doused him in petrol from a jerry can. The smell filled the warehouse.

From the floor Mr. Elm raised his pistol and shot Mr. Cedar dead. He crawled closer to Doyle and told him he was a cop, that the police were waiting outside for Bram, that help was coming if he just held on.

Cal returned, listened to Elm’s ragged account of what Cedar had done, and without a word shot Doyle dead himself. The body jerked once and went still.

Bram arrived last, looked at the corpses and the blood, and named Mr. Elm as the informer. Mr. Ash refused to believe it. He turned his gun on Bram. Cal raised his own. The three-way standoff cracked open in gunfire that left Bram, Cal, and Ash all shot. Only Ash and Elm still breathed, both leaking onto the concrete.

Elm confessed that he was a police officer. Ash stared at him a long second, then shot him. As the police stormed the warehouse doors, automatic fire cut Ash down where he stood.

Aaron Vale sat in the cardiologist’s office and heard the sentence that ended the life he knew. His heart was failing; without a donor he would be dead within weeks. Della, the wife who had already left him in every way that mattered, came to the hospital the next afternoon and pressed a consent form into his hands. She wanted his frozen sperm. She wanted a child from him before he vanished. He signed because it was easier than arguing with the dead.

Across the city Wes Tarrow stacked lumber under a hard sun. Newly born again, he kept the job, coached a boys’ baseball team on Saturdays, and tried to outrun the temper that had once put him in prison. At home his wife Nita watched him the way people watch a storm that might or might not break. She dreaded the sermons that poured out of him and the sudden white heat in his eyes when the world disappointed him.

Lena Ward had already survived her own storms. Clean for three years, she lived in a quiet subdivision with Doug and their two young daughters. Mornings smelled of coffee and crayons. She believed the worst was behind her.

On a clear Thursday afternoon Wes’s pickup reached the school crossing at the same moment Doug and the girls stepped off the curb. The impact was brief and absolute. Wes braked, stared at the stillness he had made, then gunned the engine. A hundred yards later he turned back, saw what could not be undone, and fled.

At the hospital a doctor told Lena that her husband and both children were dead. She nodded as if the words belonged to someone else.

Doug’s heart was cut free and flown across town. When Aaron woke, the new heart was already beating inside him—strong, foreign, alive. For the first time in months he drew a full breath.

Wes walked into a police station two days later and confessed. The judge sent him back to prison without ceremony.

Lena went home to an empty house and found the old hunger waiting. She bought cocaine and began the careful work of erasing herself—missed days, unpaid bills, the slow ruin of every clean thing she had built.

Aaron could not stop feeling the stranger’s heart. He hired a private investigator, learned the widow’s name, and began to follow her. He engineered a meeting at a public pool, offered a towel, a drink, a listening silence. Grief recognized grief. They became lovers in afternoon motel rooms that smelled of chlorine and regret.

He left Della a short note and told her he did not want the child she was trying to conceive. The words felt like another kind of murder.

One night he told Lena the truth: the heart keeping him alive had belonged to Doug. She struck him, threw him out, then opened the door again at three in the morning because the alternative was worse.

Wes was released early. He walked out on Nita and on the God who had failed to keep him from the road that day. He took a night clerk’s job at a motel far from everything he knew.

Lena learned where he was. She looked at Aaron with eyes that had gone flat and said, “Kill him.” Aaron bought a revolver and drove through the dark until he found the right door. He fired once. The bullet tore Wes’s shoulder. Aaron lowered the gun and told him to run.

Wes did not run far. He followed them back to their own motel, stepped into the room bleeding, and asked Aaron to finish it. Aaron turned the muzzle against his own chest instead and pulled the trigger.

They got him to the hospital while the borrowed heart still fluttered. It failed on the table. Wes, bandaged and silent, went home to Nita and the boys who still needed a coach. Lena, already carrying Aaron’s child, drove back to the empty house alone.

Ruben shared a cramped house with his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor's wife Alma and their baby. Nights brought the sound of Nestor returning from pharmacy robberies and the sharper noise of him beating Alma. Ruben began pressing her to run away with him, whispering promises while the baby slept. He discovered that Nestor's rottweiler Tigre killed other dogs on sight and started entering the animal in the local dogfights. Tigre won steadily, filling Ruben's pockets.

Ruben paid two thugs to beat Nestor. His brother answered by taking Alma, the baby and Ruben's hidden savings and vanishing into the city. Alone with the dog, Ruben kept fighting him until the last match, when the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring. Ruben stabbed Chaco and fled with his friend Pipo, Tigre bleeding in the back of the car. He ran a red light at speed and ploughed into another vehicle.

That car belonged to the model Celine Vaz. Her lover Hector had walked out on his wife and daughters and moved her into a new flat facing her own billboard. At the junction Cardo, a former guerrilla turned vagrant contract killer, dragged the bleeding Tigre from the wreck before vanishing with the dog.

Celine woke in hospital with her leg pinned together and her lapdog Chispa lost somewhere in the new flat. The little dog fell through a hole in the floorboards. Hector tore up the boards searching while Celine's leg turned gangrenous. Surgeons amputated it and the billboard carrying her image came down.

Nestor was shot dead robbing a bank. At the funeral Alma stood rigid beside the coffin and refused Ruben's last offer to leave with him.

Cardo nursed Tigre back to health among his own pack of strays. The businessman Elian hired him to murder his half-brother and business partner Sergio. Between jobs Cardo watched from a distance as his estranged wife was buried, then followed his grown daughter Perla home. While he was out, Tigre killed every other dog in the yard. Cardo put a gun to the rottweiler's head and could not fire.

He abducted Sergio but chained him in his lair instead of killing him. Later he brought Elian face to face with his brother, left a loaded pistol between them, and walked out having taken money from both. That night Cardo broke into Perla's flat, left a long confession of who he was on her answering machine and took her photograph. Shaved and in clean clothes, he left his money for her and walked out into the wasteland with Tigre.

Solly Two Coats and his crew dressed as devout pilgrims and walked into the diamond house in the northern port. They left with a huge stone tucked away as if it were nothing more than a holy relic. Overseas, his cousin Marv sent word at once: bring the stone straight over, no delays. 

In the city Grigor the Nail cornered Solly with talk of easy money at a bookmaker’s, while at the same moment he tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno that Solly would be there ripe for the taking. Meanwhile the boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam out to a travellers’ camp to buy a caravan. The bare-knuckle man Finn took offence at the deal and knocked Sam cold, leaving Halloway short a fighter for the gang boss Coldstone’s fixed bout. Halloway had no choice but to put Finn in instead and promised Coldstone the man would go down in the fourth.

Solly landed, delivered the stone to the fence Hersch, and headed straight for the bookmaker’s to lay his bets on the fight. Ike, Benno and Tulley bungled the robbery, seizing Solly’s arm and the case before Grigor chased them off. In the ring Finn knocked his opponent out cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and took it out on Halloway with fists and threats.

Marv flew in, found Solly gone, and hired the bounty hunter Ledge to track him. Grigor already had Solly. He cut the arm off to force the case open and discovered the stone was not inside. Ledge traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces and took both men and the stone. Coldstone fed what was left of Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong.

Halloway and Digby ordered Finn to go down in the fourth. That same night Coldstone’s men burned Finn’s mother to death in her caravan. Grigor ambushed Ledge’s car with Ike and Benno still inside; in the shootout Ledge, Grigor and Benno all died. Tulley slipped away with the dog that had swallowed the diamond.

In the fourth round Finn knocked his man out again. The travellers rose from the crowd and massacred Coldstone’s men. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone and shot him dead. By morning the travellers had vanished. The dog was handed in at a pet shop, coughed up the diamond, and Halloway and Digby ended up holding it.

Helicopters droned through the night, spraying the city for crop pests, their lights sweeping every neighbourhood below in slow, methodical passes. In one of those houses Doctor Neil Hartigan adjusted his tie while his wife Bess, a painter, chose earrings for the dinner party they were hosting later. Across town the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake meant for a boy named Charlie Rill, noting the delivery date without much interest.

Charlie was walking to school when a car driven by a waitress called Rhona knocked him down. He got up, brushed off his clothes, and insisted he was fine all the way home. That evening he collapsed into a coma. His parents Grant and Elaine kept vigil at the hospital, holding his hands through the long hours. Grant’s estranged father Duff appeared unannounced, sat in the corner, and confessed an affair from decades earlier that still sat between them like unfinished business. Meanwhile Otto, unpaid and ignored after the cake went uncollected, began making anonymous menacing phone calls to the family, his voice low and cryptic in the small hours.

In another living room Cheryl, a telephone-sex worker, talked men through their fantasies while her husband Stu seethed on the couch beside her, the receiver’s cord stretched taut. The next morning Stu and three friends drove out to fish. They found a young woman’s body face down in the river. They tethered it to the bank with fishing line and carried on casting for two more days before telling anyone. When Vern finally told his wife Iris, a party clown still in greasepaint from a children’s party, she was disgusted and left the room without speaking.

Night after night the singer Vida performed in a smoky club while her cellist daughter Bee practised alone at home, the bow drawing long notes against the empty walls. Officer Rowe, cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan, abandoned the family dog on a roadside to cover one of his lies, watching it disappear into the dark. Nan’s ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot who sometimes flew the pest-spray runs, learned she had a new man and went to her apartment with a saw, reducing the furniture to splinters.

Ike and Dot house-sat for the Hartigans. One afternoon they photographed Dot made up as a beaten corpse, the flash popping against the borrowed furniture. That same evening at the dinner party Bess admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and an affair. Neil made a scene, voice rising until the guests fell silent and the wine glasses trembled.

Charlie died in the hospital. Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to confront Otto. He fed them warm bread fresh from the oven and stood with them in the flour-dusted quiet, grieving as if the boy had been his own. Elsewhere Bee found her mother Vida asleep on the couch after a late set. She closed the garage door, started the car, and sat in the driver’s seat until the engine fumes took her. At a picnic in the hills Stu, still carrying the river’s secret, smashed a young woman’s head with a rock when she wandered too near their blanket.

A tremor shook the entire city at dusk. Windows rattled, power lines swayed, and every death and every wreck was folded into one evening bulletin that crackled from radios and televisions in houses still settling under the lingering chemical mist.

At the party in the house of his closest friend, while the other guests drank and laughed downstairs, Wilder led Odile up the narrow staircase to an unused bedroom. He closed the door softly and told her how lovely she was, the words plain and unadorned, as if he had been saving them for years. She did not pull away.

Soon afterward they rented two quiet rooms in a district far from either of their usual paths. They filled the cupboards with linen and the shelves with plates and glasses, giving the affair a household of its own. The afternoons there took on the unhurried rhythm of a second life.

One day Odile told him she was carrying her husband’s child. They sat with the news between them for a long minute, then decided the rented rooms would go on exactly as before. Nothing need change.

Months later, in a hotel abroad, Emlyn asked about a letter that had been held for her at the desk. He recognised the hand at once. Odile confessed everything. Emlyn listened without raising his voice and remarked, almost mildly, that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife.

When she returned she went straight to the rented rooms and said nothing whatever about the trip. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had, with tea and the same careful talk.

Emlyn, for his part, drank through a long restaurant lunch with Wilder, baiting him about the emptiness of contemporary fiction, never once mentioning what he had learned. Later, over dinner at the married couple’s house, the two men discussed racquet games and the schoolboy sports of their youth until Odile had no part in the talk at all. She cleared the plates in silence.

In time Wilder and Odile decided the rented rooms had become a chore. They split the crockery between them and surrendered the lease without ceremony.

Two years afterwards, in a bar, Odile told Wilder her marriage was over. She had spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband again, as if the first confession had never happened. Then she let slip that Emlyn had been publishing a writer whom Wilder represented and whom the two men both quietly detested.

Wilder rang Emlyn in a state. Emlyn came to his house the same evening. He stood in the doorway and said he had known for four years, that his wife had told him on the trip abroad, and that he had never thought much of his friend’s letters either.

I hadn't slept in months. The only thing that worked was sitting in basement support groups for diseases I didn't have, letting strangers cry on my shoulder until the tears came and knocked me out cold. Then Ada Vey showed up. She faked it worse than I did, chain-smoking through testicular cancer and blood parasites, and her smirk ruined every meeting. Without the release I was raw again, staring at ceiling cracks until dawn.

On a red-eye flight to investigate a faulty toaster recall I sat beside a soap salesman named Rex Marrow. He talked about the purity of rendered fat and the emptiness of catalogue living. I pocketed his card when we landed. That same week my flat exploded—gas main, they said—taking every stick of particle-board furniture with it. I dialed the number. Rex pulled up in a dented sedan and drove me to a leaking wreck at the edge of the industrial district. Rain came through the roof; we slept on the floorboards.

Outside a bar one night he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. I did. He hit back. We beat each other bloody in the gravel until the cops rolled past and we laughed like idiots. The brawls hardened into a weekly thing in the house basement. Rules appeared: no shirts, no shoes, fights end when one man taps out. Men queued up. We called it the club and it grew.

Ada overdosed on Xanax in a motel. Rex brought her to the house and they started fucking loud enough to shake the pipes. I hated the sounds, hated how she looked at him. Meanwhile Rex raided a liposuction clinic dumpster, rendered the stolen fat into clean white bars, and sold them back to department stores for eighty dollars each. One night he poured lye across my hand and held it there while I screamed, refusing to let me drift into the calm place I used when pain got too big. “This is the greatest moment of your life,” he said, “and you’re missing it.”

I showed up at the recall office with my face swollen purple and blackmailed my boss into paying me to stay home. Full salary, no questions. Rex shaved the new recruits and named the whole circus Havoc. They took orders, smashed satellite dishes, glued billboards, turned corporate lobbies into abstract art. One night he floored the accelerator into oncoming headlights, let the car tumble, then vanished from the wreck while I bled in the ditch.

A kid named Ogden caught a security guard’s bullet on a paint-bomb run. I tried to shut Havoc down after that, but every city I reached already had a basement full of bruised men who clapped me on the shoulder and called me Rex Marrow. The truth surfaced slowly: I was him. While I slept he drove, fought, fucked, recruited. Ada confirmed it without blinking—she had only ever slept with me.

I found the plans. Havoc had packed the foundations of the debt-record towers with homemade plastique. I raced through stairwells cutting wires until Rex caught me, slammed me down flight after flight, laughing with my own mouth. At the bottom I jammed the pistol between my teeth and pulled the trigger, blowing a hole through my cheek to silence him. Blood filled my throat but he was gone.

The shaven men delivered Ada to the observation deck. We held hands at the floor-to-ceiling glass while the charges bloomed one after another, the towers folding in on themselves like exhausted lungs, paper records fluttering down through the dark like confetti for a wedding no one attended.

The shaven men delivered Ada to the observation deck. We held hands at the floor-to-ceiling glass while the charges bloomed one after another, the towers folding in on themselves like exhausted lungs, paper records fluttering down through the dark like confetti for a wedding no one attended.

A boy was born in a small industrial town and grew into a weak, peculiar child who never quite fit the rough edges of the place. One afternoon his father decided to teach him to swim the only way he knew how and flung him into the deep end of the municipal pool. The boy sank straight to the bottom and stayed there until someone hauled him out coughing and blue.

Years later he was conscripted as a chaplain’s assistant and shipped overseas with no training worth the name. Behind the lines he became lost with a scout who beat him bloody for wanting to be left to die in the snow. The pair were captured soon after. On the prison train the scout’s wound turned to gangrene; with his last breath he blamed the peculiar boy for everything and died.

In the camp he was held beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through a simple clerical error no one ever corrected. Later he was sent on to a great city and housed with other prisoners in a disused abattoir. That night the city was destroyed by fire. When the prisoners climbed out of the meat locker they found only ash and skeletons of buildings where streets had been.

They were put to work digging bodies out of the cellars. One of the diggers worked until the dry heaves killed him where he stood. A fellow prisoner, remembering the dead scout, promised the peculiar man that one day he would have him killed on that account.

He came home, collapsed, and was hospitalised. In the next bed another patient introduced him to the novels of a hack science-fiction writer whose wild inventions somehow made more sense than the war. In time he married the daughter of the man who owned the optometry school and, through that alliance, became rich.

He survived an air crash in the mountains, but his wife, racing to the hospital, died of exhaust fumes leaking into her car. Not long afterward he was taken by aliens and kept in a zoo on their planet together with a film actress. The aliens calmly explained that every moment exists at once and that free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet; they found the notion charming and primitive.

Back on Earth he went on a radio talk show and tried to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension. His daughter decided he was senile and took his affairs out of his hands. One afternoon he addressed a crowd beneath an open sky. He had always known the instant would arrive. A beam weapon took him cleanly through the forehead and he crumpled, exactly as he had always known he would.

Lise lay beside Cort in the narrow bed, her voice low as she described the dream that kept returning: a red tunnel stretching endlessly ahead, walls pulsing like living flesh, drawing her deeper with every step. Cort traced idle circles on her shoulder and teased that maybe Jonah still haunted her sleep, the ex who had left her restless. She laughed and jabbed him lightly, saying Jonah would never last a night in any tunnel of hers, and Cort grinned back, claiming he alone knew the way through.

Alone the next afternoon in the flat, Lise locked the bathroom door and waited out the minutes on the plastic stick. The second line bloomed clear and dark. She sat on the closed lid staring at it until the numbers on the display stopped mattering.

Later she carried a book to the park and found a bench where sprinklers arced silver water over bright grass. Children shrieked and chased one another through the spray. One of her hands rested lightly on her stomach while she turned pages she scarcely read.

That evening the three of them rode the underground toward the party. Lise sat between Cort and Jonah as the train rattled. They argued cheerfully about whose turn it was to buy the next round, about the ethics of casual sex, about how many drinks Cort could handle before he became impossible. Jonah claimed Cort already smelled of last night’s whiskey; Cort shot back that Jonah still carried a torch large enough to light the whole carriage. Lise smiled at both of them and said nothing about the test.

At the flat where the party spilled from room to room, Cort drank steadily and smoked whatever was passed to him. His eyes grew glassy. He drifted toward a cluster of women near the speakers, leaning in too close, laughing too loud. Disgust settled cold in Lise’s chest. She slipped out without saying goodbye and started the walk home alone.

Rather than wait for a gap in the traffic on the busy road she chose the pedestrian underpass. Halfway down the concrete slope she heard the wet sound of fists and a woman’s broken sobs. A tall man the street called the Adder was beating a transsexual woman against the tiled wall, kicking her when she folded. Lise froze. The Adder turned, saw her, and the underpass became a red tunnel of pain. He forced her down, raped her on the filthy floor, then gripped her hair and slammed her head against the concrete again and again. A passer-by appeared at the far entrance, took one look, and backed away into the night.

Cort and Jonah pushed out of the party sometime after midnight and found the ambulance already there, blue lights washing the pavement. Paramedics were loading Lise’s still form onto a stretcher. Blood matted her hair. Cort tried to climb in after her and was held back.

Two men drifted up from the shadows while the ambulance doors closed. They spoke softly to Cort, offering a name for a price, the name of the man who had done this. They pointed him and Jonah toward a club called the Pit and melted away again.

Inside the Pit the air was thick with smoke and bass. Cort shoved through the crowd hunting for the face the men had described. He seized a stranger by the jacket, certain he had the right one. The stranger twisted, braced, and snapped Cort’s arm with a clean, brutal motion. Cort went to his knees white-faced. Jonah grabbed a fire extinguisher from the wall and swung it into the stranger’s face once, twice, until bone gave and blood sprayed. A few feet away the real Adder stood watching, expressionless, then slipped deeper into the dark.

Police poured in, forced Cort and Jonah to the floor, snapped cuffs on their wrists, and carried the pair out into the street under the orange sodium lights.

High above that same street, in a flat whose window overlooked the flashing lights and the gathering crowd, an old man sat with a younger one and spoke quietly. Nothing survives time, he said. Not flesh, not fury, not the names we give our wounds. The younger man listened as the sirens faded below.
